claims.text: Classical or machine-learning interatomic potentials combined with two-phase coexistence molecular dynamics can reasonably predict melting temperature, entropy and enthalpy of fusion, and volume change at melting for refractory alloys.
Potential-driven molecular dynamics can provide these melting properties in high-throughput calculations without the prohibitive cost of ab initio free-energy methods.
The target refractory alloy is initially as-cast or as-synthesized and lacks significant prior thermal or mechanical processing that could alter its microstructure.
Extensive molecular dynamics simulations of a refractory alloy can be driven by a highly accurate machine-learning interatomic potential.
Classical interatomic potentials can be used for molecular dynamics simulations of chemically complex high-entropy alloys.
Two-phase molecular dynamics can assess solid-liquid coexistence over a specified temperature range.
Simulations at multiple temperatures with sufficient equilibration can accurately characterize phase coexistence and its thermodynamic quantities.
Solid-liquid interfaces form and stabilize under constant-temperature and constant-pressure conditions in the simulated volume.
Atomistic interactions represented by an accurate potential allow the simulated system to reach equilibrium coexistence of solid and liquid phases.
Melting temperature, latent heat, volume change, and entropy of melting can be derived from an equilibrium two-phase simulation.
The proposed method will produce computationally tractable and reliable estimates of high-temperature melting properties.
The resulting estimates can enable effective screening of refractory alloys for high-performance applications.
Ab initio free-energy simulations are accurate but too computationally expensive for high-throughput materials discovery.
The reliability of predicted melting behavior depends on the quality and transferability of the interatomic potential for high-temperature, chemically complex refractory alloys.
Short-range ordering can materially affect behavior in refractory high-entropy alloys and therefore may cause variability if it is not captured by the potential.
Complex phase behavior or insufficient sampling may introduce variability into predicted melting properties.
The hypothesis can be tested by applying the method to refractory alloys with experimentally known melting curves and comparing predicted and measured properties.
Failure to remain within accepted experimental uncertainties or to reproduce qualitative melting behavior across multiple alloys would refute the hypothesis.
